channel.title: Unlock your homelab from your phone on Server Hands

item.title: Homelab setup
item.description:
1. BIOS: Restore on AC power loss = Power On; enable Wake-on-LAN. DHCP reservation for the server.
  2. Install the package, either from the apt repository (preferred, gives upgrades: see the apt repository page) or from a downloaded file: sudo apt install ./server-hands_X.Y.Z_amd64.deb
  3. sudo handsctl discover --write, then review labels and the [post_unlock] lists in /etc/server-hands/config.toml. Drives with an /etc/crypttab entry are skipped and reported.
  4. Add a phone-only keyslot per drive (you will be prompted for the existing passphrase; the new one is generated and shown once for entry into the app): sudo handsctl add-phone-key <luks-uuid> (libcryptsetup directly; the existing passphrase is read from the tty, nothing goes through argv)
  5. Post-unlock actions. Docker and the other services are not gated: they start at boot as usual. Containers that need the encrypted drives are started by scripts instead, so containers that only use the root disk are unaffected.

    • Stop the dependent containers from starting at boot, so they do not come up on empty mount points: set restart: "no" in their compose files (or docker update --restart=no <container>) so the script is the only thing that starts them.

    • Put the commands in a script, e.g. start from /usr/share/server-hands/post-unlock-example.sh:

      It must be owned by root and not writable by anyone else (its directory too), and must not be under /home. handsd refuses to run it otherwise.

    • Register it in /etc/server-hands/config.toml:

      Manual scripts do not have to be about the unlock: add requires_unlock = false to one (a status check, a service restart, a reboot) and the app can run it at any time, even while the drives are locked. Without it a manual script is refused until every drive is unlocked.

      For dangerous scripts (a reboot, say) add requires_confirmation = true (the app asks “Run X?”) or biometric_protection = true (the phone must produce a fresh fingerprint/face, which the server checks with a challenge it issues; the biometric prompt then replaces the dialog). The first protected run registers the phone’s approval key automatically. If the phone’s biometrics change, the key is destroyed; run sudo handsctl reset-approval-key <device-id> (ids from handsctl devices) and the phone registers a new one on its next protected run. Scripts run as root in a transient unit, in the order listed, after the pool is refreshed. A non-zero exit or the timeout_secs limit (default 300) shows as “failed” in the app. Output: journalctl -u server-hands-script-media.

    • Test it without a reboot: sudo systemctl restart handsd, unlock (or, with the drives already open, handsd runs auto scripts at startup), then check the app’s “Scripts” card.

    • The mergerfs pool: list its mount unit in mount_units. To get the value (run these with the drives unlocked and the pool mounted):

      If findmnt prints nothing, the pool is not mounted; the pool’s name is on the OMV web UI’s Storage > Union Filesystems page, and the mount point is /srv/mergerfs/<name> (check with ls /srv/mergerfs). Then put the unit name in the config:

      The same list feeds the pool bar in the app, so a wrong name shows as “Not mounted” there. After the drives are mounted handsd runs systemctl restart on it, exactly as the OMV mergerfs plugin’s “restart pool” action does. If something holds the pool open (a running container or Samba), the restart can fail with “target is busy”; keep those out of boot, or start them from a script.

    • service_units takes plain systemd unit names (systemctl list-unit-files | grep -i smb finds them, e.g. smbd.service); they are started without waiting after the unlock. Prefer a script for containers.

    • Optional hard gating of a systemd service (the old approach): sudo install -D -m644 /usr/share/server-hands/gated-service.conf /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/server-hands.conf, add the unit to service_units.

  6. sudo systemctl enable --now handsd.socket handsd.service, then run systemd-analyze security handsd.service and expect an exposure of 3.0 or lower.
  7. sudo handsctl pair, scan the QR in the app, confirm the 6-digit code on both sides.
  8. Shorter boot delay (optional, recommended). The locked drives’ fstab entries make systemd wait for their devices for the default 90 s before giving up, which stalls boot. Lower the default device timeout:
    This sets DefaultDeviceTimeoutSec=10s in [Manager]. It is global (every device wait in fstab, also USB or network disks), so use a larger value if you have slow-appearing disks. OMV regenerates /etc/fstab, so per-entry x-systemd.device-timeout= options would be overwritten; the global setting survives. Check the effect after a reboot with systemd-analyze blame | head and systemd-analyze critical-chain. To undo: delete the file and systemctl daemon-reexec.
  9. Reboot, open the app, approve. Check the OMV GUI shows the drives unlocked and mounted.

item.title: Apt repository
item.description: The GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/deb.yml) builds the package in a Debian 13 container on every push and pull request and uploads it as a workflow artifact (server-hands-deb, plus SHA256SUMS; hands-client-linux-amd64 is the test client). Pushing a tag v* (for example v0.5.0) additionally publishes the package to a signed apt repository served from GitHub Pages, so the server can install and upgrade it with plain apt.

item.title: Android app release
item.description: The app workflow (.github/workflows/app.yml) tests the app and builds an APK on every push and pull request. On a tag vX.Y.Z it builds a signed release APK and attaches it, with SHA256SUMS, to the GitHub Release of that tag (created if missing). The same tag also drives the server package (deb workflow), so one tag releases both. The tag sets versionName (v0.5.0 gives 0.5.0) and versionCode (major*10000 + minor*100 + patch, e.g. 500).

item.title: Protocol v1
item.description:
Single version, no negotiation, no fallback. Anything else is rejected.

Keys

Key Algorithm Where Purpose
Server identity S Ed25519 /var/lib/server-hands/identity.key (0600, root) signs every server message; pinned by clients
Server TLS key ECDSA P-256 self-signed cert state dir transport only; SPKI SHA-256 pinned by clients
Request ephemeral E X25519 RAM only, one per request HPKE recipient key; destroyed after approval
Device identity D ECDSA P-256 Android Keystore (StrongBox preferred), non-exportable, setUnlockedDeviceRequired signs approvals; public key stored on server at pairing
Approval key A ECDSA P-256 Android Keystore (StrongBox preferred), non-exportable, per-use strong biometric (setUserAuthenticationRequired, timeout 0, invalidated by new enrolment) signs script approvals; public key registered on the server, one per device
Vault key AES-256-GCM Android Keystore, per-use biometric encrypts the passphrase vault blob

Primitives: HPKE RFC 9180 base mode, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305. Hash: SHA-256. Randomness: OS CSPRNG.

item.title: Threat model
item.description:
Assets: LUKS passphrases (phone vault, in flight, server RAM during unlock); server identity key; paired-device list.

# Threat Mitigation
T1 Attacker on LAN impersonates server (ARP/DNS spoof, rogue AP, replayed old replies) QR out-of-band trust root; pinned TLS SPKI + pinned Ed25519 identity; fresh client nonce in every signed reply; no TOFU after pairing; no address from mDNS/intents/push
T2 Fake server asks for other drives’ passphrases Vault releases only UUIDs recorded for that server; HPKE info binds server key, req, nonce, device
T3 Network eavesdropper TLS plus independent HPKE to a per-request ephemeral key (forward secret)
T4 Stolen/unlocked phone Per-use BiometricPrompt + CryptoObject, BIOMETRIC_STRONG only, key invalidated on new enrollment; revoke device + kill phone keyslot
T5 Malware on phone Keystore/StrongBox non-exportable keys; passphrases in memory only briefly as zeroed ByteArray; FLAG_SECURE; no backups; overlay protection; no accessibility-visible passphrase text
T6 Secrets leaking via logs/ps/core/swap on server libcryptsetup (no argv), pipes not files, Secret newtypes, no body logging, LimitCORE=0, PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0, MemorySwapMax=0, mlockall (swap is unencrypted)
T7 Replay of a recorded approve Single-use nonce, request consumed on first decrypt, ephemeral key destroyed, 10-min expiry
T8 Brute force on approve endpoint Device-signed requests only, rate limit/backoff, constant-shape errors
T9 Rogue pairing One-time 5-min token, QR only via SSH console, SAS confirmed by operator
T10 Server host compromise (root) Out of scope: root can read the passphrase during unlock. Limit blast radius with a dedicated phone keyslot
T11 Supply chain Signed releases, cargo-deny, pinned Gradle dependency verification, SBOM, reproducible builds
T12 Phone (or a stolen paired key) used to run arbitrary commands via post-unlock scripts The phone only names a script from the server’s config, never a path or arguments; scripts must be root-owned and not group/world-writable (checked before every run); run requests are device-signed with single-use nonces; scripts only start once all drives are unlocked unless the script sets requires_unlock = false
T13 Someone with the unlocked phone runs a dangerous script (for example a reboot) with one tap Per script: requires_confirmation (app dialog, convenience only) and biometric_protection (server enforced: the run needs a signature from a Keystore key that needs a fresh strong biometric, over a single-use 60 s challenge the server issued for that device and script; no replay, no reuse for another script, no pre-signing). The approval key is registered once and cannot be swapped by the phone; the operator resets it. Limit: the server trusts the app to have created the key as biometric-bound (no attestation check yet), so a rooted phone or modified app is out of scope
T14 Machine details (hostname, uptime, load, memory, disk usage) leak to someone on the LAN /v1/status is a device-signed request, so only paired phones get an answer, and the reply travels inside pinned TLS. It is read-only and carries no secrets. To read the global /proc files handsd runs without ProcSubset=pid (other processes stay hidden with ProtectProc=invisible)
